tagline.text: The volcanic cliff "the Rockies," overlooking Taal Lake

image.credit: Lawrence Ruiz / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A volcano rising about

above sea level south of Taal Lake, known for the lake views from its sheer rock face, "the Rockies." However, all hiking has been banned since early 2020, so for now it's a mountain to be admired from the village of Cuenca below and the lakeshore, rather than climbed.
Mount Maculot (also called Mount Macolod) is a dormant volcano rising about

in Cuenca, Batangas province. It's the highest point on the southern rim of the Taal Caldera, and is believed to be a volcanic edifice that predates the massive eruption that formed the caldera tens of thousands of years ago. Standing on the Tagaytay ridge, you can see this very mountain rising beyond Taal Volcano Island, on the far side of the lake.
The mountain's icon is "the Rockies," a massive volcanic rock face dropping toward the lake from about

up. Standing at the cliff's edge, Taal Lake and its volcanic island unfold below like a painting, with the Tagaytay ridge in the distance — long ranked as one of the finest viewpoints for hiking in southern Luzon. Partway up the mountain is a grotto shrine to the Virgin Mary, and it was also a mountain of faith, climbed each Holy Week by many pilgrims as an act of penance.
However, following the Taal Volcano eruption and the spread of COVID-19 in early

, the Cuenca local government issued an administrative order closing the mountain to hikers, and the closure has continued since, citing forest restoration, capacity assessment, and the drafting of a new tourism management ordinance. The closure covers the entire mountain, including the Rockies, the summit, and the grotto, and even the Holy Week pilgrimage hike is not allowed. No reopening date has been announced.

So for now, Mount Maculot is a mountain "to view," not "to climb." A realistic trip is to stop in Cuenca village at the mountain's foot during a drive around Taal Lake, try the old church and a bowl of Batangas-style lomi, and admire the mountain's imposing shape from the lakeshore or the hills toward Lipa. Hiking enthusiasts waiting for word of reopening may want to look up the old route in advance.

From the viewpoints along the Tagaytay ridge, Mount Maculot rises beyond Taal Volcano Island, on the far side of the lake. It's the classic Taal Lake view, layering the lake, the volcano, and the mountain.

blocks.title: Stroll Cuenca village at the mountain's foot

children.text: A quiet rural village with the mountain standing behind it like a screen. From anywhere in the village, the cliff and ridge loom close overhead, so you get a real sense of the mountain's scale even without climbing it.
Cuenca Church, in the center of the village, is a Gothic-style church built in the late 19th century, dedicated to San Isidro, the patron saint of farmers. Its white twin-tower facade is striking.
Cuenca and neighboring Lipa are the home of lomi, thick noodles in a rich, starchy broth. Try it at a village lomi shop, seasoned to taste with soy sauce, calamansi, and chili flakes.

blocks.title: A drive along the south side of Taal Lake

children.text: The road from Cuenca through Alitagtag to Taal Heritage Town makes for a drive that takes in mountain, lake, and old town together. The mountain's shape shifts depending on your angle.
About 30 minutes away by car, Lipa is the home of kapeng barako, a strong, bitter Batangas coffee. Round off your trip with a cup, the mountain visible in the distance.

blocks.title: Hike the Rockies once it reopens

children.text: This is the first thing to do once hiking is allowed again. The view of Taal Lake from the cliff-top viewpoint, at the end of a steep forest trail, has long been ranked one of the finest scenes in southern Luzon hiking.

Cuenca town proper is walkable, and a tricycle covers short distances slightly farther out for about
. To also tour Taal Heritage Town and Lipa, it's more efficient to charter a tricycle for half a day or use a car.
For a clear view of the mountain, the dry season,
November–April
, is best.
December–February

in particular has clear, cool air, with many days offering a clean view of the whole mountain from Tagaytay and the lakeshore. Clouds tend to gather on the summit in the afternoon, so morning is better for photos.
In the
June–October

rainy season, the mountain turns a deep green but is often hidden by cloud and rain, and travel along the lakeshore roads gets inconvenient when a typhoon passes through. If the Taal Volcano alert level rises, some areas around the lake are restricted, so check announcements from the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS).

late March–April

Cuenca is a small farming village, so there aren't many places to stay. A few resorts at the mountain's foot offer views of the peak, at about

per night, and there are also pool resorts for a weekend family outing. For more options, it's convenient to stay at a hotel in Lipa town, about 30 minutes away by car, or a place in Tagaytay with views of Taal Lake, and visit as a day trip.

Be sure to try lomi if you're in Cuenca. It's a Batangas-style noodle dish, thick egg noodles in a broth thickened with egg and starch, piled high with pork, liver, and fish cake, seasoned to taste with soy sauce, calamansi, chopped onion, and chili flakes. In Lipa, try strong kapeng barako coffee, and at restaurants toward Batangas City, bulalo beef bone soup. If you make it to Taal Heritage Town, Taal-style empanada and fried longganisa sausage are also famous there.
Hiking reports and price information from before 2019 that are still online date from before the closure. Be sure to check the latest notice from the Cuenca tourism office before you go.
To take in the whole mountain in one shot, the Tagaytay ridge on the far side of the lake or the hills toward Lipa work well. A telephoto lens can even capture the Rockies cliff face.
Combining it with Taal Heritage Town, Lipa, and Tagaytay into a full day around Taal Lake makes the travel time worthwhile.
If taking the bus, tell the conductor in advance that you're getting off in "Cuenca." Some routes to Lemery don't pass through Cuenca.
Lomi shops get busy from late morning, and some close in the late afternoon, so time your visit for lunch.
The mountain is often clouded over in the afternoon. If photos are your goal, arrive early in the morning.
If reopening is announced, expect a rush of hikers in the early days. A weekday visit and booking a guide in advance are recommended.

Mount Maculot has been closed to all hiking, including the Rockies, the summit, and the grotto, since early 2020, and no reopening date has been announced. The Cuenca tourism office has stated that rumors of partial reopening are false, so don't attempt to hike without authorization.
Bypassing the closure via village back trails or a private, unofficial guide is subject to enforcement, and rescue and insurance become very difficult if an accident occurs.
Even Holy Week pilgrimage hikes are not permitted. If you wish to make a pilgrimage, join the liturgy at the village church instead.
If the Taal Volcano alert level rises, areas around the lake are restricted, and there may be effects from volcanic gas or ash. Check PHIVOLCS announcements.
Once hiking resumes, note that the edge of the Rockies is an unguarded drop. Don't stand at the cliff's edge for a photo.
Before the closure, the trail had no water source along the way and included a rope section. Once it reopens, bring plenty of water and gloves.
